title: Tulane University Study Abroad Record 2018: In a City Overflowing with Music
paragraphs: "Today again, gazing at the high blue sky, I walk along the main street where old-fashioned streetcars come and go. When I turn into the second alley from Bourbon Street, the first thing that jumps into my ears is the sound of trombones and saxophones. My back is sweating in the strong sunlight, and I thought of getting a cold coffee to quench my thirst, but I keep stopping in my tracks at the live jazz heard everywhere, so I can hardly get a drink. Before I know it I am absorbed and finish listening to a third band, say "bravo!!" in my heart and toss a dollar bill into the bucket. And then I notice that the sky has changed completely and looks odd. It is a cloudy sky like gray and black paint stirred together. Within a few minutes the sweat on my upper body is washed away by large drops of water, and I immediately take refuge in a nearby cafe. I am absorbed in the piano performance I encounter here too, and by the time I notice, the orange sunlight has already stretched to the foot of the piano, so I decide to resume my walk toward the great river of the South. Walking along the embankment, the wind hitting my body is strong and my body is already completely dry. The whistle of a steamboat moored at the edge of the brown, muddy, rapid current was playing a famous song by this city's great master, and it was lovely. What a wonderful world!"

In New Orleans I often spent weekends like this. I took part in clinical clerkships at Tulane University, in the "city of music" where on holidays one wants to go out and "listen to" the city. During the preparation before the clerkship and during the clerkship at Tulane University, I ran into many difficulties. I struggled with the strong accents of patients and doctors, keeping up with conversation was very stressful, and sometimes I collapsed onto my bed exhausted when I got back to my room. But I think it was thanks to the "help" of cheerful music that I was able to overcome these difficulties by acting boldly and actively. (Really.)

In New Orleans, when it was still a little chilly, my first clerkship department was hematology/oncology. Perhaps because I was excited and nervous about my first clinical clerkship in the United States, my first greeting was full of stumbles. When I asked for a greeting Take 2, the fellow doctor and the students laughed and forgave me, and I feel that it became a good icebreaker. The student clerkship in this department was to belong to the consult team and think about the treatment plans for inpatients together with the fellow. In hematology/oncology there are various teams (a benign hematology group, a leukemia group, a solid tumor team and so on), and I took part in the solid tumor team. The students' first job was early: quickly doing the assessment of inpatients and sorting out the problem list. What needed to be asked was basically the same as in clerkships in Japan, but I struggled with the patients' various expressions and their local accents, and took more than twice as long. After the discussion time we visited the patients with the fellow, confirmed the information again, and then in the second discussion time we examined the plan. What I struggled with here was that I could not come up with as many ideas for treatment strategy as the local students. I could keep up with the discussion and fire off questions, but I could not discuss with ideas of my own, and I felt frustrated.

When the wind on my skin had grown warm, my next rotation was orthopedics. I had heard that mornings in American surgical fields are early, and I had seen scenes of rousing patients awake on early-morning rounds in American medical dramas several times, so I felt "well prepared, fully ready." However, going out on rounds while it was still pitch dark, and after about an hour of conference, with operations starting just when it finally seemed to have become light, more than half of my stamina had already been taken by the dense morning work hours. Orthopedics has four groups, sports, trauma, pediatric and reconstruction, and I was allowed to learn in each group for one week each. There were many gunshot cases, and I was allowed to study the management of fractures and gunshot wounds in the orthopedic trauma group, and seeing gunshot wounds and fractures that one can almost never encounter in Japan was a good experience (something to tell stories about).

After more than a month in New Orleans, I had gotten quite used to the clerkship and life. I took on famous New Orleans foods such as beignets (frightfully sweet fried pastries) and po'boys (hearty catfish sandwiches), but the one thing I kept avoiding was crawfish (after all, they are crayfish). At the crawfish party I went to with my Tulane friends, I felt just a little relief that it was sold out, and I was a little intimidated by the remains of crawfish heads piled up all over the outdoors. After that I ended up meeting crawfish again at a dinner party I was invited to, so this time I took one with a determined spirit. Their shells, boiled in strong spices, were red and hard, and when I peeled one off with effort, what could be eaten was smaller than the size of an index finger. The spice flavor was strong, and it did not taste as much like shrimp as I had imagined. I was told that the reason crawfish are more popular even though the seafood caught around New Orleans is plentiful (shrimp are of course delicious too) is that it is New Orleans culture. By slowly taking time to extract the hard-to-eat, small bits of meat, they create time to enjoy small talk. I felt that it is a food culture rooted in the relaxed atmosphere and life of the people of New Orleans.

When the new fourth-year students of the Tulane University School of Medicine finished taking USMLE Step 2 and joined new elective clerkships, the department I went to next was ophthalmology. I ended up studying in a department that was unexpected as a clerkship site, and I struggled quite a lot with the medical terminology peculiar to ophthalmology, but with the support of the students and residents who rotated with me, there was much to learn and it was a very fruitful clerkship. Because in the outpatient clinic I was entrusted with new patients, I also struggled with how to use the ophthalmoscope and slit lamp, but I was able to see many typical findings of diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, cataract and so on. And when it became the season when the heat clinging to the body and the slightly painful sunlight sap one's strength, my clerkship at Tulane University came to its last rotation. The last was an outpatient clerkship in Family medicine. Because it is a department that comprehensively sees patients with various diseases and problems, I spent quite a lot of time on information gathering. The various clinical skills I had learned until then were useful, and I was very happy to receive words of praise from the attending doctor.

This study abroad at Tulane University was more fulfilling and satisfying than my earlier study abroad experiences. I was able to deepen friendships not only with local students but also with Japanese doctors and researchers who are striving and doing well in foreign lands, and I felt anew that all kinds of people support one another and strive every day toward their goals. This experience has become a great foundation and a source of motivation toward my new goals. I am deeply grateful to the doctors, family and friends who supported this study abroad.
